subject: Pathology
summary: Leber Hereditary Optic Neuropathy (LHON) is a mitochondrial DNA disorder causing painless, acute loss of central vision in young adults. It follows a classic pattern of bilateral, sequential optic nerve degeneration.

sections.p: LHON is a maternally inherited mitochondrial mutation leading to loss of retinal ganglion cells. Diagnosis requires clinical history, visual field testing, and confirmation of a pathogenic mtDNA mutation (e.g., 11778G>A).
b: Painless, subacute central vision loss; often starts in one eye then the other within weeks to months.

t.b: Measures degree of vision loss; a sudden drop supports LHON.
Shows central scotoma; confirms optic neuropathy.
Detects thinning of retinal nerve fiber layer; indicates optic nerve damage.
Identifies pathogenic mutation; confirms diagnosis when clinical picture fits.

sections.p: Staging is based on visual acuity and time from onset. Early stage: acuity 20/200–20/400; intermediate: 20/400–20/800; late: <20/800 or complete blindness.
b: Early stage: rapid recovery possible; later stages have poor prognosis.

sections.p: The most common cause is the 11778G>A mutation in MT-ND4. Other pathogenic variants include 3460G>A and 14484T>C. Environmental triggers such as smoking or alcohol can precipitate onset.

t.b: Maternal relatives with visual loss suggest LHON.

sections.p: Patients report sudden, painless loss of central vision, often after a stressful event. The first eye is affected, followed by the second eye within weeks. Color vision may be reduced.
b: No pain, no eye redness, no systemic symptoms.

sections.p: Key tests confirm optic nerve involvement and rule out other causes. In low-resource settings, basic visual acuity and field testing are essential.

t.b: Shows optic disc pallor; confirms optic nerve damage.

t.b: Rule out vitamin B12 deficiency, thyroid disease, or infections.

sections.p: Rapid deterioration, pain, or associated neurological signs suggest alternative diagnoses such as optic neuritis or compressive lesions.
b: Painful vision loss, eye redness, or systemic infection symptoms.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden vision loss with pain, eye redness, or systemic infection symptoms

faq.a: There is no cure; treatment focuses on prevention and supportive care.

faq.q: Does it affect both eyes equally?
faq.a: It usually starts in one eye and affects the other within weeks to months, but severity can vary.
Yes, it is maternally inherited through mitochondrial DNA mutations.
